555.t: Shadings and dynamics in her arrangements
555.s: Liston writes at the piano or keyboard, still uses shadings, tells drummers dynamics rather than notating, and links it to Miss Hightower's lessons.
555.q: I don’t know of anybody that’s doing that, but I don’t hear Benny Golson’s and Randy – I mean Ernie’s – I don’t hear those things, so I don’t know whether they’re doing that or not.

555.s: Liston thinks long, then writes nearly straight through and edits repeatedly; she writes for the drums as well.

1036.t: Early arranging mistakes: writing too much
1036.s: Looking back on Glenn Miller days, he learned not to write everything and to think in colors and combinations; recalls hearing his first symphony.

215.t: Favorite arrangers and the value of lyrics
215.s: Praise for Johnny Mandel and Robert Farnon, and Rodgers and Schwartz and Dietz lyrics.
215.q: No but if you want to hear great arrangements, listen to anything Johnny Mandel wrote or Robert Farnon who was the daddy of all the arrangers. He’s got some great albums, Schwartz and Dietz songs, made in England, unbelievable orchestrations.

751.t: Writing by hand and thinking about the players
751.s: Hand-written scores yield voicings tried at the piano and parts that are fun to play, a lineage from Rayburn Wright.

153.t: Knowing instrument ranges and giving the band rests
153.s: His father made him study trumpet, trombone and sax so he knew their ranges, and he writes rests, avoids constant fortissimo and thinks of the soloists.
153.q: To create an arrangement – I’m going back to my early days with my dad in the music store.
